You report what others said at B2 level using a variety of reporting verbs (asegurar, admitir, reconocer, confesar, negar, prometer, advertir, reprochar, sugerir, quejarse de, recordar, insistir en) and choose the correct mood after each verb: indicative (aseguró que era…), subjunctive (le reprochó que no hubiera llamado, negó que fuera verdad) or conditional (prometió que volvería).
Costel promised him he would study with him again.
Mr Dan admitted he was very nervous.
Ana reminded him he had been only two points short.
The teacher warned her that there was no Spanish class in first grade.
To use reporting verbs that take the indicative: asegurar, afirmar, admitir, reconocer, confesar, explicar, contar.
To use verbs expressing a promise or prediction with the future or conditional: prometer que vendrá / que vendría.
To use verbs that take the subjunctive: negar que, reprochar que, quejarse de que, lamentar que, and the influence verbs sugerir, recomendar, insistir en que.
To distinguish "advertir que + indicative" (to inform) from "advertir que + subjunctive" (to warn someone to do something), and "recordar que + indicative" from "recordar que + subjunctive".
To summarise a whole conversation with the right verbs, without repeating "dijo que" all the time.
Monday, 28 September, morning. The C1 results are out. Costel has passed. Mr Dan has not, by two points. Ana is trying to console him. Costel has just arrived.
Fifty-eight. I was two points short. And there I was, assuring everyone that the C1 was a matter of method.
Dan, the oral examiner told me you spoke very well. Let me remind you that you hardly slept the night before.
I admit it. I was thinking about Grandpa. In the writing paper I lost the thread for five minutes.
Dan, forgive me. I know it's not the moment, but… I passed. With sixty-three.
Don't apologise to me. You've earned it. I never doubted you would pass.
There's another session in November. I suggest you sit it again. Two points are nothing.
And I promise you I'll study with you every Thursday, in the cab, as always.
Precisely because of that. Last year you promised me you wouldn't leave me alone with the subjunctive. Now it's my turn.
Then it's decided. And I don't want to hear anyone complaining that the exam was unfair.
"te recuerdo que" = let me remind you that
"te lo has ganado" = you've earned it
"nunca he dudado de que" = I never doubted that
"me toca a mí" = it's my turn
The diphthong "ie" appears under stress: ad-VIER-to, but ad-ver-TIR. Likewise: sugerir → su-GIE-ro, confesar → con-FIE-so.
"ch" as in English "church": re-pro-CHAR. Stress on the last syllable in the infinitive: re-pro-CHAR, in the present: re-PRO-cho.
Stress on "to": con-vo-ca-TO-ria. Five syllables; the diphthong "ria" is pronounced as one.
Aseguró que el examen era cuestión de método.
Confesó que nunca le había gustado vender.
Le explicó que había otra convocatoria.
to remind someone of a fact
Le recordó que casi no había dormido.
With these verbs, apply the reported-speech rules from chapter 70: present → imperfect, perfect → pluperfect, future → conditional.
"I will study with you." → He promised him he would study with him.
"I will return to Madrid." → He promised he would return to Madrid.
He has promised me he will come to the wedding. (a recent promise, still valid)
I never doubted you would pass.

If the main verb is in the present perfect (me ha prometido), you can keep the future: «Me ha prometido que vendrá». If it is in the preterite (me prometió), use the conditional: «Me prometió que vendría».
Le reprochó que no lo hubiera llamado.
Se quejó de que el examen fuera injusto.
Le sugirió que se presentara otra vez.
to insist that someone do something
"No negar que" takes the indicative, because it acknowledges the fact: «No niego que tienes razón». "Negar que" without negation takes the subjunctive: «Niego que tenga razón».
Le advirtió que no había clase de español. (informed)
Le advirtió que no llegara tarde. (warned not to…)
Le recordó que había dormido poco. (fact)
Le recordó que trajera el libro. (to do something)

Andrei sums up for Ecaterina, in an email, Faustino's last day at the stall on the Cuesta de Moyano. Notice the reporting verbs.
Dear Ecaterina, yesterday was Faustino's last day on the Cuesta de Moyano. He confessed to me that he had never liked selling books, that what he liked was talking about them.
He gave Lucas the keys to the stall and warned him that the Sunday customers were the most difficult. Lucas promised he would look after it as if it were his own.
I asked him if he was sad. He denied it. He maintained that at his age he only got sad over bad books, and that in Triana many good ones were waiting for him.
At the end, he insisted that I send you his regards and reminded you that you owe him a visit to Triana. He says he accepts no excuses. A hug, Andrei.
Que nunca le había gustado vender libros
Que cuidaría la caseta como si fuera suya
Que le debía una visita a Triana
Que tenía que escribir otro libro

On 14 September, Rosa Elena started school. It was the preparatory class, the first year of real school, with desks, a bell and a new teacher called Mrs Ionescu, like Ecaterina, although they were not related. Rosa Elena arrived on the first day with her new school bag, her camera hanging round her neck and a prepared statement: she told the teacher, in front of the whole class, that she taught Spanish lessons on Fridays. The teacher warned her that there was no Spanish class at school, that this was not kindergarten. Rosa Elena insisted she think about it. The teacher promised she would. Rosa Elena told her mother that afternoon that in Spanish this was called "una victoria".

The first week of school was not easy. On Tuesday, Mrs Ionescu asked Ana to talk to her at pick-up time. She told her that Rosa Elena had complained, in front of everyone, that nobody in the class could say "hola". That she had reproached a classmate for not thanking her for lending him a pencil, and that when the boy answered that he didn't understand what she was saying, she had suggested, very politely, that he learn. Ana apologised. The teacher assured her there was no need, and confessed that in twenty years of teaching she had never had a pupil who corrected her in two languages.

In Madrid, Andrei marked one year on 31 August. It was exactly a year since he had landed at Barajas with two suitcases, three cameras and a little bag of soil from under a walnut tree. Begoña said nothing that day, because Begoña never remembered anniversaries. But the following Monday she called him into her office and told him that this month he could choose his own assignment, whatever he wanted. Andrei did not hesitate. He told her he wanted to photograph Faustino's last day on the Cuesta de Moyano. Begoña asked whether Faustino was going somewhere. Andrei explained that he was going to Seville, to get married. Begoña fell silent for a moment and said that this was something she really hadn't seen coming.

Before Andrei left the office, Begoña reproached him for something. She told him that in a whole year he had not once asked for a pay rise, and that in a photo agency this was almost an insult. Andrei answered that he hadn't dared. Begoña reminded him that she didn't bite, at least not on Mondays. Then she confessed that she had spoken to the management in July, without telling him, and that from October he would be paid as a staff photographer. Andrei didn't know what to say. Begoña warned him that if he thanked her, she would take it back. Andrei didn't thank her. He thanked Lucas, who laughed for five minutes.

Faustino's last day at the stall was Sunday, 20 September. He had been selling books in that same spot for sixty-three years, since he was twenty-four. Andrei arrived at nine in the morning with the film camera Begoña had given him for Christmas. Faustino was already there, in his red beret, arranging the books on the wooden shelves for the last time, one by one, very slowly. Andrei asked him if he was sad. Faustino denied it. He maintained that at his age he only got sad over bad books, and that in Triana many good ones were waiting for him.

Throughout the morning the regular customers came, one after another. A retired teacher who had bought a history book from him every Sunday since 1980. A lady who had sold him her husband's library when he died, and who sometimes came to buy back one of those books, to have it at home again. A young man who had started reading at that stall at the age of twelve and was now a literature teacher at a secondary school in Vallecas. They all asked him the same thing, and he gave them all the same answer: that he was going to Seville, that he was getting married and that no, he did not intend to come back, because at his age you don't leave in order to come back.

At eleven Marta turned up, her hair a mess and with dark circles under her eyes, because she had been writing until five in the morning. She reproached Faustino for not telling her the exact date; she had found out from Andrei the night before. Faustino answered that he hadn't told anyone precisely so that nobody would come. Marta assured him she had no intention of leaving. She sat on a folding chair next to the stall, took out her notebook and spent the morning writing down everything the customers said. Faustino complained that they were turning him into a character in a novel. Marta reminded him that he had been one for a year.

Around midday, while they ate a sandwich sitting on the stool, Faustino confessed to Andrei something he had never told anyone. He told him he had never liked selling books. That what he liked was talking about them, and that selling had only been the excuse for people to stop and talk to him. That in sixty-three years he had sold perhaps a hundred thousand books, but he remembered very few of them. What he remembered were the conversations. Andrei asked him whether he was sorry to leave all that behind. Faustino admitted that he was, a little. But he added that in Triana there was a bookseller who talked even more than he did.

After lunch Lola from El Mostrador came by with a cardboard box under her arm. It held ten of the letters that had reached the newspaper after Ecaterina's article, the ones that mentioned the Cuesta de Moyano. She explained to Faustino that several readers said they had bought there, decades ago, the book in which they had kept a letter they never sent. Faustino read them all, one by one, with his glasses on the tip of his nose. When he finished he admitted he did not remember any of those customers. But he added that he was glad he had sold them the right book.

In the afternoon Lucas arrived. Faustino had decided to hand the stall over to him for a symbolic price: one euro and the promise that he would never close it on a Sunday. Lucas, who had been looking after it at weekends all summer, had accepted without a second thought, although he wasn't quite sure how he would combine it with his job at the agency. When Begoña found out, she told him that as long as he was at his desk at nine on Mondays, as far as she was concerned he could sell books, tortillas or whatever he liked. Faustino gave him the keys and warned him that the Sunday customers were the most difficult. Lucas promised he would look after the stall as if it were his own. Faustino reminded him that, from that moment on, it was.

The last thing Faustino did before leaving was take down the framed five-hundred-peseta note and the photo of Andrés he had hung next to it. He wrapped them in newspaper and put them in his cloth bag, together with the beret for special occasions. Lucas asked him whether he didn't want to leave the note at the stall, as a keepsake. Faustino answered no, that the note was the payment of a debt, and that paid debts had to be taken home. Then he shook Lucas's hand, hugged Andrei and walked off towards Atocha, very slowly, without looking back. Andrei took a single photo: his back, walking away, with the red beret.

Andrei developed the film that same evening in the agency's darkroom. Of the thirty-six photos he had taken, only one seemed truly good to him: the last one, of Faustino's back walking away towards Atocha. On Monday morning he showed it to Begoña without saying anything. Begoña looked at it for a long time. Then she assured him it was the best photo he had taken in a year, and suggested he send it to Marta, because it wasn't a photo, it was the cover of a novel. Andrei asked her how she knew. Begoña answered that thirty years of craft couldn't be learned in one, however much talent you had.

That evening Andrei wrote Ecaterina an email summing up the day. He told her that Faustino had confessed he had never liked selling books, that he had given the keys to Lucas, that he had denied being sad and that, at the end, he had insisted that Andrei send her his regards and had reminded her that she owed him a visit to Triana. Ecaterina replied the next morning that Faustino was right, that she owed him a visit, and that she intended to pay it in October, at the wedding, with interest. Andrei asked her what interest. Ecaterina told him a book by Neruda, of course.

Marta, meanwhile, finished the first draft of her novel on 25 September at four in the morning. It was called "La librera de Triana" and had two hundred and forty pages. She sent it to Inés that same morning, with a note warning her that the ending might still change, because the real protagonists had not yet married. Inés replied that she would read it that week and suggested she change nothing until after the wedding. Marta asked her why. Inés explained that the best endings, in her experience, were written after things had happened, not before.

Ecaterina, for her part, was discovering what it was like to be on the other side of a translation. The Italian translator from Turin, a young woman named Chiara, wrote to her every week with questions. She asked her what exactly "pues muy bien" meant in Andrés's mouth, how to translate "the green sign" without losing the colour, whether "La Lámpara" should stay in Spanish or be translated as "La Lampada". Ecaterina answered patiently, remembering the hundreds of emails she herself had sent for forty years to authors who didn't always reply. She assured Chiara she could ask her anything. And she suggested she leave "La Lámpara" in Spanish, because some names are not translated: they are kept.

One afternoon, Chiara confessed to Ecaterina something that was worrying her. She told her that while translating the lamp chapter she had cried three times, and she was afraid it would show in the Italian, that the translation would come out too sentimental. Ecaterina answered that she had cried five times writing it, and nobody had complained. She assured her that a translation didn't have to be cold to be faithful. But she warned her, before sending the text to the publisher, to read it aloud the next day, once calm, and to remove only the adjectives that had cried along with her.

The C1 exam results came out on Monday, 28 September. This time nobody had to wait until seven: Ana had persuaded Mr Dan to check the website at nine, with a coffee in front of him and his wife beside him. Costel was on the road, near Brașov. Mr Dan logged in first. He read his name, his candidate number and, in the last column, two words instead of one: NO APTO. Underneath, the score: fifty-eight. He had been two points short. His wife took his hand. Mr Dan said nothing for a long while. Then he admitted, very quietly, that he hadn't expected it.

It was his wife who spoke first. She reminded him that two points were exactly the difference between one question answered correctly and one answered wrongly, nothing more. She also reminded him that a year earlier he couldn't tell the subjunctive from the conditional, and that now he had come so close to a C1 that the academy would have to invent a new level for him. Mr Dan smiled a little, half-heartedly. He admitted she was right. But he complained that the exam had been on the same weekend as Grandpa's stretcher, and then he immediately regretted it, because he acknowledged it was nobody's fault.

Costel found out half an hour later, at a petrol station, by phone. Ana read him his own score first, because Mr Dan had insisted that he be told before his own: pass, sixty-three. He had passed by three points. Costel didn't cry this time. He stood silent, looking at the pumps, and then asked about Mr Dan. Ana told him what had happened. Costel told her he was on his way. Ana warned him he was three hours away. Costel replied that, in that case, he would be there in three hours. And he got there in two and a half, although nobody wanted to ask him how.

On the way, Costel called his daughter in Valencia. She already knew, because Ana had sent her a message with a single word in capitals: APTO. She told him she was proud of him and promised they would celebrate that evening by video call, with Álex. Then she passed the phone to Álex, who assured him, in his school Spanish, that he had already said in July that he would eat it with chips. Costel reminded him that Mr Dan had not passed. Álex was quiet for a moment. Then he suggested Costel take him something to eat, because, in his experience, failed exams were easier to bear on a full stomach.

When Costel arrived at Mr Dan's house, he found him in the garage, once again repairing the old bicycle nobody used. Costel apologised. He told him he knew it wasn't the moment, but he had passed. Mr Dan put the spanner down on the table and told him not to apologise, that he had earned it. That he had never doubted he would pass. And that if anyone had to apologise, it was him, for losing the thread for five minutes in the writing paper thinking about Grandpa Gheorghe on the stretcher. Costel reminded him that from that stretcher Grandpa had ordered them to go to the exam. Mr Dan admitted that, at least, he had obeyed.

Ana arrived a little later, with her notebook. She reminded Mr Dan that the oral examiner had told him, on the way out, that he had spoken very well, and that there was another session in November. She suggested he sit it again. Mr Dan hesitated. He said it might not be worth it, that at his age a C1 was of no use to him. Costel answered that it was of no use to him either, and that this was precisely why it had been worth it. Then he promised he would study with him every Thursday, in the cab, as always. Mr Dan asked him whether he would, even though he had already passed. Costel told him: precisely because of that.

He reminded him of one thing: that a year earlier, in November, when he had been ready to give it all up because the subjunctive wouldn't go into his head, Mr Dan had promised him he wouldn't leave him alone with the subjunctive. "Now it's my turn," he told him. Mr Dan stood looking at the bicycle. Then he took a sheet of paper from the workbench and began to draw a table: weeks left until November, hours of study per week, points to recover in each paper. Ana and Costel looked at each other. Ana said quietly that this meant yes. Costel said it meant that Mr Dan was back.

Costel followed Álex's advice. Before leaving, he went out to the bakery on the corner and came back with a bag of warm covrigi. The three of them ate them in the garage, sitting on toolboxes, while Mr Dan finished his table. Ana asked him which part of the exam he planned to prepare first. Mr Dan answered the writing paper, of course, and that this time he wouldn't think of anyone while he wrote. Costel warned him that this was impossible. Mr Dan admitted that yes, it probably was. In that case, he said, he would think of someone on purpose, from the start, so as not to lose the thread halfway through.

That same afternoon, Costel drove to Grandpa Gheorghe's village with a printed sheet in his hand: the provisional C1 certificate, which could be downloaded from the website until the real diploma arrived, which would take several months. Grandpa was on the porch, under the walnut tree, with the oil lamp ready for seven. Costel handed him the sheet without saying anything. Grandpa looked at it for a long time, although he couldn't read it, because it was in Spanish. Then he got up, went into the house, took down the empty frame Costel had given him in August, put the sheet inside and hung it back on the wall. Costel told him it was only provisional. Grandpa answered that, at his age, everything was.

Then Grandpa asked about Mr Dan. Costel told him he had failed by two points and was going to sit the exam again in November. Grandpa thought for a while. Then he asked Costel to give Mr Dan a message from him, word for word. Costel promised he would. Grandpa said: "Tell him I learned to read at thirty, and that the first time I tried, I failed too." Costel asked him if it was true. Grandpa confessed that it wasn't, that he had just made it up. But he insisted that Costel tell him anyway, because some lies help more than many truths.

The following Thursday, in the truck cab, Costel gave Mr Dan Grandpa's message, word for word, as he had promised. Mr Dan listened in silence. Then he asked whether it was true that Grandpa had failed the first time. Costel confessed that it wasn't, that Grandpa himself had admitted he had made it up. Mr Dan was silent for a moment and then burst out laughing, for the first time since Monday, a long laugh that made the steering wheel shake. He said it was the most honest lie he had ever been told. And he opened the exercise book at the first page.

At seven, Grandpa lit the oil lamp. Costel stayed for dinner. Rosa Elena, who had come to the village with her father as soon as she heard about the certificate, showed Costel her new school notebook, with the first letters she had learned to write in Romanian. At the end of the last page, without anyone asking her, she had written a sentence in Spanish in crooked letters: "The teacher said she would think about it." Costel asked her what it meant. Rosa Elena explained, very seriously, that in her experience, when a teacher said she would think about it, it meant yes, but she didn't know it yet.
¿Qué le advirtió la profesora a Rosa Elena?
Que en el colegio no había clase de español
Que no podía llevar la cámara
¿Por cuánto le traspasó Faustino la caseta a Lucas?
Por un euro y una promesa
¿Qué hizo el abuelo con el certificado provisional?
Lo metió en el marco vacío y lo colgó

The Italian translator writes to Ecaterina. Ecaterina then sums up the email for Inés.
Inés, Chiara, the Italian translator, wrote to me today. She confessed she has been stuck for three days on the phrase "pues muy bien".

She complains that in Italian it sounds either too enthusiastic or too cold. I suggested she not look for the exact translation, but for the tone of a grandfather who doesn't want anyone to notice he is happy.
She has promised to send me three options on Friday. I warned her that I probably won't like any of them. After all, it took me forty years to translate that phrase. Ecaterina.
"que se note" = for it to show

Que busque el tono, no la traducción exacta
